_note: Short summaries of what is known about each species, shown on the site under the timeline. Edit freely; each species is keyed by its slug in scripts/build_data.py.

mediterranean-house-gecko.native: Mediterranean region and the Middle East
mediterranean-house-gecko.moves: In cargo, vehicles and trailers; one reached Missouri in a travel trailer bought in Florida
mediterranean-house-gecko.lives: Outside walls of buildings, especially near lights at night
known: Active at night and closely tied to buildings, which stay warmer than the surrounding air in winter.
Its range edge has moved north through Louisiana, Oklahoma and Tennessee over recent decades.
In southern Florida the tropical house gecko appears to be replacing it.
unknown: Where its northern limit lies, and how far heated buildings let it go past that limit.
How many northern records are breeding populations and how many are single hitchhikers.
Whether the tropical house gecko will push it out of the Gulf Coast as well.
refs: Locey and Stone (2006), Journal of Herpetology 40: 526–530

tropical-house-gecko.arrived: Southern Florida, increasingly common since about 1990
tropical-house-gecko.moves: In freight, lumber and potted plants; it may have crossed the Atlantic to South America before human shipping
tropical-house-gecko.lives: Buildings, and more often than other house geckos, rural and undeveloped areas
known: On buildings in southern Florida it outnumbers the Indo-Pacific gecko.
It appears to be displacing the Mediterranean house gecko across most of southern Florida.
It is rapidly expanding its range northward in Florida.
unknown: How much winter cold it can survive, and so how far north it can spread.
Whether it will replace the Mediterranean house gecko outside Florida.

indo-pacific-gecko.native: South and Southeast Asia, Australia and the Pacific islands
known: Every individual is female; eggs develop without fertilization (parthenogenesis), so one gecko can start a population.
On Florida buildings the tropical house gecko usually outnumbers it, but where Cuban treefrogs are present it can come out ahead.
unknown: Why it persists in some places where the tropical house gecko has arrived.
How far north it can establish.

brown-anole.arrived: Florida Keys, late 1800s; now across the Gulf states
brown-anole.moves: Especially in nursery plants, and in vehicles
brown-anole.lives: Ground and low branches in open, disturbed and urban areas
brown-anole.eats: Insects and spiders; also smaller lizards, including young green anoles
known: Where it arrives, native green anoles move higher into trees. On Florida islands, green anoles evolved larger toe pads for climbing within about 15 years.
Its range has expanded faster since the 1970s and now covers a much wider span of latitude than its native range.
Invasive populations measured along its range show little change in cold tolerance with climate.
unknown: Whether its cold tolerance can evolve fast enough to support further spread north.
How far north the plant trade will keep moving it.

northern-curly-tailed-lizard.native: Cuba, the Bahamas and nearby islands
northern-curly-tailed-lizard.arrived: Palm Beach, Florida, 1940s; reportedly 20 pairs released to control insects
northern-curly-tailed-lizard.moves: Released and moved by people; spread slowly outward from Palm Beach
northern-curly-tailed-lizard.lives: Open, sunny, sandy or rocky ground; concrete and seawalls in cities
northern-curly-tailed-lizard.eats: Insects, small lizards including anoles, and some flowers
known: By 1959 it had spread about 20 city blocks; by 1968, a few kilometers along the coast.
A 2005 study predicted frost would keep populations unstable north of Fort Pierce; records now reach north Florida and southern Georgia.
unknown: Whether the records in Georgia and the Carolinas are breeding populations.
How it affects native lizards where it becomes common.
refs: Smith and Engeman (2004), Florida Field Naturalist 32: 107–113

italian-wall-lizard.arrived: Long Island, New York, 1967; also Topeka, Kansas, and parts of California
italian-wall-lizard.moves: Mainly through the pet trade and deliberate releases
italian-wall-lizard.lives: Walls, rock piles, rail beds and gardens in cities and suburbs
known: Genetic studies trace California populations to Sicily and the Kansas and New York populations to Tuscany.
It tolerates colder winters than the tropical lizards on this site.
unknown: Whether it is spreading much beyond its original release sites; published assessments disagree.
How city life affects its body, behavior and genetics, an active research question in New York.

common-wall-lizard.arrived: Cincinnati, Ohio, 1951; brought from northern Italy by a boy on a family trip (accounts of the details vary)
common-wall-lizard.moves: Along railroad tracks, and moved by people to new parts of the region
common-wall-lizard.lives: Stone walls, railroad tracks and rocky, south-facing slopes
known: Genetic work suggests the Cincinnati population descends from as few as three founders.
It has survived record-setting cold winters, and now lives in pockets across Cincinnati and into Kentucky and Indiana.
Railroad tracks have played a part in its spread.
unknown: How far along rail lines it can travel, and how fast.
Whether it competes with Ohio's native lizards and skinks.

brahminy-blind-snake.arrived: Florida, by the late 1900s; now in several southern states
brahminy-blind-snake.moves: In the soil of potted plants; it is now on every continent except Antarctica
brahminy-blind-snake.lives: Underground, in soil, leaf litter and flowerpots
brahminy-blind-snake.eats: Eggs, larvae and pupae of ants and termites
known: Every individual is female and reproduces without mating, so one snake in one flowerpot can start a population.
At about 15 cm long, it is often mistaken for an earthworm.
unknown: How many of its records are established populations and how many are single snakes arriving in plant shipments.
How often it goes unnoticed, which affects how its spread can be measured.
What effect it has on native soil animals.

cuban-treefrog.native: Cuba, the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands
cuban-treefrog.moves: In potted plants, vehicles and shipping
cuban-treefrog.lives: Trees, buildings and wet areas; the largest treefrog in North America
cuban-treefrog.eats: Insects, other frogs including native treefrogs, and small lizards such as geckos
known: Native treefrogs tend to become less common where it is abundant.
It preys on house geckos, which can change which gecko species dominates a building.
Its skin secretions irritate eyes and cuts.
unknown: How much winter cold it can survive.
Whether frogs found outside Florida are breeding populations or hitchhikers.

cane-toad.native: Southern Texas through Mexico, Central America and South America
cane-toad.arrived: Florida, 1930s for sugarcane pest control, with a larger population traced to a release at Miami's airport in 1955
cane-toad.moves: Released by people; spreads along canals and through suburbs
cane-toad.lives: Lawns, canals, golf courses and other open ground near water
cane-toad.eats: Almost anything it can swallow, including insects and pet food
known: Its toxic skin secretions can sicken or kill dogs that bite it.
Records in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas are its native range, not a spread.
Scientists now often split it into two species, so some Texas records are filed under Rhinella horribilis.
unknown: How far north in Florida it can survive winters.
How the change in its scientific name affects counts built from databases like GBIF.

spotted-lanternfly.moves: Egg masses laid on vehicles, rail cars, stone and outdoor gear; adults also ride on vehicles
spotted-lanternfly.lives: Trees and vines; it strongly prefers tree-of-heaven, itself an invasive tree common along roads and railways
spotted-lanternfly.eats: Sap of dozens of plant species, including grapevines
known: Simulations point to cars, trucks and trains as the main drivers of its spread across the eastern US.
One modeling study links infestation to primary Interstate highways specifically, not to road density in general.
Many states have run campaigns asking people to report and kill it, which raises the number of records.
unknown: How far into colder or hotter climates it can establish.
How much its record counts reflect reporting campaigns and how much its actual spread.
